correctness.rationale: Under the stated bMGP Gaussian limits, whitening the sampling error by the posterior covariance produces the weighted chi-square law \(Q=\sum_i(1+\lambda_i)^{-1}Z_i^2\). The exact ellipsoid scalar follows from continuity and strict monotonicity of this law; the all-contrast threshold follows from the extremal generalized Rayleigh quotient. Strict anisotropic bounds and the high-confidence limit follow from pathwise chi-square comparisons. The proportionality converse follows by equality of moment-generating functions. The result is explicitly asymptotic and does not infer an infinite statement from finite computation.

originality.rationale: Tanaka (2026) already covers the generic facts that scalar posterior calibration is level-specific and that all-level Gaussian calibration requires proportional sampling and posterior covariance, so those statements were removed from the originality claim. The surviving claim is narrower: under the bMGP covariance decomposition, the exact scalar for a chosen joint Gaussian ellipsoid is a weighted-chi-square quantile ratio that is strictly below the sharp all-linear-contrast non-undercoverage threshold under anisotropy, and the two thresholds coalesce at extreme confidence. No inspected bMGP, generalized-posterior calibration, bagging, or matrix-adjustment source states this joint-versus-contrast frontier.
residual_risks: Tanaka (2026) is very close structurally; although the inspected accessible text does not state the surviving joint-versus-all-contrast frontier, an equivalent observation could appear elsewhere in the paper under different notation.
Weighted-chi-square covariance-mismatch calculations and generalized-eigenvalue extremality are classical ingredients, so equivalent scalar-constrained consequences may exist under other terminology.
Matrix-valued posterior calibration is scientifically stronger when full covariance adjustment is permitted; the claim is restricted to scalar radial post-processing.

value.rationale: The bMGP deliberately gains calibration by adding bootstrap variability, so the practical cost is excess width. The theorem gives an exact, level-specific way to remove as much scalar excess as possible for a joint ellipsoid without rerunning predictive simulations or estimating a rotation, and it proves when this goal conflicts with protecting every contrast. The two-dimensional example shows a substantial strict gap: exact 95 percent joint calibration at about \(\tau=0.69177\) while all-contrast protection requires \(\tau=1\). This is a motivated structural boundary, not an arbitrary numerical slice.
